title: Pressure-cooker whole chicken
subtitle: Juicy, evenly cooked, and ready in 25 minutes
excerpt: A whole chicken cooked under pressure with stock and aromatics. The result is exceptionally moist, better for eating cold or shredding than roasting, with a built-in broth from the cooking liquid.
sourceNotes: Pressure-cooking a whole chicken is a method found across French and Italian domestic cooking, where the technique was used to speed up a Sunday bird without roasting. The cooking liquid becomes a usable broth.

recipe.freezeNotes: Shred the cooked chicken and freeze in airtight containers with a little broth for up to 3 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The chicken can be cooked ahead, cooled in the broth, and refrigerated for up to 3 days. Slice cold or reheat gently covered in broth.

content.text: A pressure-cooker whole chicken does not crisp its skin, you will not get that from a sealed, steamy environment, but it produces the most consistently moist chicken you can make at home. The breast and thigh cook evenly together, neither drying out, in about 25 minutes at high pressure.

Think of this chicken as a component rather than a centrepiece. It is the starting point for a dozen dishes: sliced cold with salad, shredded into tacos or sandwiches, folded into a pie with the broth. The cooking liquid is a genuine, lightly flavoured broth that can be used anywhere chicken stock is needed.
Check the size of your pressure cooker before starting. A 1.5 kg chicken fits in a 6-litre pot. A larger bird needs a bigger cooker, or joint it before cooking.

Season the chicken all over with salt and pepper, including inside the cavity. Put the onion, carrot, celery, garlic, thyme, and bay leaf in the base of the pressure cooker. Set the chicken on top, breast side up. Pour in {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock, it should come at least 3 cm up the sides of the pot.

Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 25 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of at least 10 minutes before opening. Do not quick-release, the chicken needs the residual heat to finish cooking evenly.

Lift the chicken out carefully, it will be fragile. Transfer to a board and rest for 10 minutes. Pierce the thigh at the thickest point: the juices should run clear, not pink. Carve and serve, or shred the meat for another use. Strain the cooking liquid and reserve as broth.

rows.cause: Insufficient cooking time, or a larger-than-expected bird.
rows.fix: Return the whole chicken to the sealed pot and cook at high pressure for a further 5 minutes. Check again before serving.

rows.symptom: The chicken falls apart on lifting
rows.cause: This is normal for a fully pressure-cooked chicken, the collagen breaks down and the flesh softens. The bird is perfectly cooked.
rows.fix: Use a wide spatula or two wooden spoons to lift it. If serving whole, lower a trivet or plate under the chicken before cooking so you can lift everything at once.

rows.symptom: The skin is pale and rubbery
rows.cause: Pressure cookers are a steamy, enclosed environment, skin cannot crisp inside them.
rows.fix: For browned skin, pat the cooked chicken dry and place under a hot grill for 3 to 4 minutes. Or embrace the pale-skin result and serve the meat removed from skin.

content.text: The pressure-cooked whole chicken is a practical rather than a showpiece dish. It suits a household that eats chicken several different ways across a week, carved for dinner, shredded for sandwiches, stock used for a soup. The 25-minute cook time makes it a viable midweek option even when roasting is not.
